chunks: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Ali ibn Ibrahim from his father from Ibn Abi Umayr from Ibn Udhaynah from Zurarah, Bukayr, al-Fadl, Muhammad ibn Muslim, and Burayd al-Ajli from Abu Ja'far and Abu Abdillah (peace be upon them) that they said:

Regarding a man who is among some of these sects (or theological schools) — al-Haruriyyah, al-Murji'ah, al-Uthmaniyyah, and al-Qadariyyah — then he repents, acknowledges this matter, and his opinion improves: does he have to repeat every prayer he prayed, or fast, or pay zakat, or perform hajj, or is he not required to repeat anything of that? He said: 'He is not required to repeat anything of that, except for zakat, and he must pay it, because he placed the zakat in its non-appropriate place, and its appropriate place is the Ahl al-Wilayah.'

key_terms.أَهْلُ الْوِلَايَةِ: The Ahl al-Wilayah (People of Authority/Guidance, referring to the Imams)
key_terms.الْأَهْوَاءِ: Theological sects or schools of thought
key_terms.الْحَرُورِيَّةِ: Al-Haruriyyah (a sect, often associated with Khawarij)
key_terms.الْقَدَرِيَّةِ: Al-Qadariyyah (a theological sect emphasizing free will)

ai.seo_question: Does a convert from a theological sect need to repeat their zakat payments?
ai.summary: This ruling from the Ahl al-Bayt highlights the distinct Shia jurisprudential view that zakat is not merely a general charity but a political-religious right of the Ahl al-Wilayah (the Imams or their deputies). Consequently, when a convert repents from sects like the Qadariyyah or Murji'ah, his previous zakat payments are considered invalid because they were given to the opposing political authority rather than the rightful recipients, necessitating repayment. This underscores the theological link between correct belief (usul al-din) and the proper administration of wealth (fiqh) in Shia tradition.
